to "for the upright in heart, gladness," as mentioned above.
As stated in the holy Zohar
And this is the power of the increase

paragraphs.text: Zohar II 152a, Terumah — “Come and see: Tes is the illumination of life in every place. Therefore the verse begins with it in 'that it was good,' as it is written: 'God saw the light, that it was good.' From this letter the destroying angel flees—or rather, he is not given permission to enter there. This letter differs from kuf: kuf is not established in any settled place in the world; its sign is 'A man of evil speech shall not be established in the land.' Tes is established in every place and is properly fitted to settle there; wherever tes is, kuf has no settled place. ... Just as this letter rules in this place, so another letter rules in the place of Gehinnom. Which is it? Qof.” The source contrasts tes with kuf in the account of a place protected from death. The retrieved text also preserves a variant reading of ches for kuf. Rav Tzadok's argument follows the kuf reading quoted in his manuscript.

paragraphs.text: Zohar II 148b, Terumah — “Everywhere, this serpent follows the mystery of the woman of valor. The woman of harlotry seeks to fashion herself in her likeness, but cannot. The mark and letter of the woman of valor is heh, and so it befits her. The mark and letter of the woman of harlotry is kuf; her letter is fashioned after the shape of heh, like an ape beside human beings: it follows human beings, yet cannot become like them.” The comparison describes imitation of holiness by its opposite. Rav Tzadok later distinguishes that counterfeit from the holy imitation of God's ways that he associates with kuf.

paragraphs.text: Bereishis Rabbah 20:1 — “Another interpretation: 'A man of evil speech'—this is the serpent, which spoke evil of its Creator. 'Shall not be established in the land'—'upon your belly.' 'A violent man, evil shall hunt him to repeated falls': it does not say one fall, but repeated falls—Adam was cursed, Chavah was cursed, and the serpent was cursed.” The Midrash explicitly identifies the evil speaker of Psalms 140:12 with the primordial serpent, linking the Zohar's proof-text to the serpent's counterfeit likeness.

paragraphs.text: Berachos 31a — “Rabbi Yochanan said in the name of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai: A person may not fill his mouth with laughter in this world, as it is said: 'Then our mouth shall be filled with laughter and our tongue with song.' When? At the time when 'they shall say among the nations: Hashem has done great things with these.' They said of Reish Lakish that he never filled his mouth with laughter in this world from the time he heard this from Rabbi Yochanan his teacher.” The Gemara itself specifies the future recognition of God's great deeds by the nations. The distinction between inward joy and laughter's full outward disclosure is developed in the following maamarim.

paragraphs.text: Berachos 61b — “The lung draws in all kinds of liquids; the liver becomes angry; the gall casts a drop into it and quiets it; the spleen laughs; the gizzard grinds; the stomach sleeps; the nose keeps awake. If the sleeper awakens and the wakeful one sleeps, the person wastes away.” Within the Gemara's account of bodily functions, 'the spleen laughs' is the particular clause used here. Sefer Yetzirah's Gra recension likewise assigns the spleen and laughter to Adar.

paragraphs.text: Tikkunei Zohar, Tikkun 48, 85a — “Happy is the person who keeps a dwelling for Shabbos—namely the heart—so that the spleen's sadness and the gall's anger, the fire of Gehinnom, do not approach there. Indeed, anyone who becomes angry is as though he kindled the fire of Gehinnom.” The source associates the spleen with sadness. Rav Tzadok brings it alongside the Gemara's 'the spleen laughs' to distinguish unstable indulgence from the holy joy developed in Adar.

paragraphs.text: Zohar I 202a, Mikeitz — “A person should recall the day of death, for this breaks the human heart. The evil inclination dwells only where there is the joy of wine and arrogance of spirit. Where a broken spirit is found, it departs and does not dwell with him. ... Come and see: the good inclination seeks the joy of Torah; the evil inclination seeks the joy of wine, adultery, and arrogance of spirit. Therefore a person should continually confront it with that great day, the day of judgment and accounting.” The source itself distinguishes two kinds of joy. Rav Tzadok therefore does not identify all joy with the spleen's unstable laughter.

paragraphs.text: Yerushalmi, Rosh Hashanah 1:3; Vayikra Rabbah 35:3 — “Rabbi Elazar said: In ordinary practice a mortal king makes a decree; if he wishes, he observes it, while others observe it. But the Holy One, blessed be He, is not so: He decrees a decree and first observes it Himself. What is the basis? 'They shall keep My charge; I am Hashem'—I am the One Who first kept the Torah's commandments. Rabbi Simon said: It is written, 'Rise before the aged and honor the elder ... I am Hashem'—I am the One Who first fulfilled standing before an elder.” The parallel Midrash in Vayikra Rabbah 35:3, also retrieved, gives the same principle. Rav Tzadok makes it the basis of 'walking in His ways': the commanded deed follows a Divine pattern.

paragraphs.text: Midrash Tanchuma, Bereishis 2, opening Sheilta — “The house of Israel is obligated to rest on Shabbos. When the Holy One, blessed be He, created the world, He created it in six days and rested on Shabbos, blessing and sanctifying it, like one who builds a house, finishes its work, and makes a festive day. ... The Merciful One says: Rest on Shabbos just as I rested on it, as it is written: 'He rested on the seventh day; therefore Hashem blessed' it.” This Aramaic opening, explicitly a Sheilta, gives the direct formulation of imitating Divine rest that Rav Tzadok quotes.

paragraphs.text: Parallel: Malbim, commentary to Tehillim 97:10–11 and Beur HaMilos to 97:11 — “‘Light is sown for the righteous’: divine light is found sown within them, like a seed planted in their souls, ready to bear fruit and multiply if they water it, tend it, and cultivate it, like a seed ready to bear fruit and multiply. For one who guards his soul and performs its service, the sown light will grow and bear fruit until it becomes sevenfold light, as it says, ‘The path of the righteous is like shining light.’ The great prophetic light will penetrate him. Through this, ‘for the upright of heart, joy’: they will rejoice with spiritual joy through the divine light shining within their souls, when His lamp shines above their heads, as it says, ‘The light of the righteous gives joy.’ In Beur HaMilos he explains: ‘For the righteous, for the upright of heart’: the righteous person conquers his inclination; the upright of heart has a nature that inclines toward good. He rejoices because he has no inward war.”

paragraphs.text: Connection: Malbim supplies both elements of Rav Tzadok's reading of this verse: light begins as something planted that grows through the person's work, and uprightness describes a heart whose inclination toward good has ended the inner conflict. This clarifies the transition from the tzaddik's conquest of the leftward heart to the yashar lev's revealed joy. It does not identify the two stages merely because both people act correctly; the decisive difference is what has happened within the heart.

paragraphs.text: Temurah 16a — “Rav Judah said in the name of Samuel: Three thousand laws were forgotten during the mourning for Moses. They said to Joshua: Ask! He answered them: ‘It is not in heaven.’ ... It was taught: One thousand seven hundred a-fortiori inferences, analogous-word derivations, and details of scribal law were forgotten during the mourning for Moses. Rabbi Avahu said: Nevertheless, Osniel ben Kenaz restored them through his dialectical analysis, as it is said: 'Osniel ben Kenaz, Kalev's brother, captured it, and he gave him Achsah his daughter as a wife.'” The preceding teaching specifies that seventeen hundred inferences, analogies, and fine points of the Scribes were forgotten during the mourning for Moshe. Later the Gemara identifies Osniel with Yaavetz and interprets Yaavetz as one who advised and disseminated Torah in Israel. Rav Tzadok sees the restoration through analysis as a birth of Oral Torah precisely at the time of loss.

paragraphs.text: Berachos 12b–13a — “They said to him: The Exodus from Egypt will not be uprooted from its place. Rather, deliverance from the subjugation of kingdoms will become the principal subject, and the Exodus from Egypt will be secondary to it.” The Sages respond to Ben Zoma's citation of Jeremiah's promise of a future ingathering from the northern land and all the lands of exile. paragraphs.text: Shabbos 30b — “'I praised joy'—this is the joy of a mitzvah. 'And of joy, what does it accomplish?'—this is joy unconnected to a mitzvah. This teaches that the Divine Presence rests neither from sadness, laziness, laughter, frivolity, conversation, nor idle matters, but from the joy of a mitzvah, as it is said: 'Now bring me a musician'; and when the musician played, the hand of Hashem came upon him.” The verse about the musician is II Kings 3:15. The passage recognizes holy joy as the setting for inspiration while distinguishing it from laughter.

paragraphs.text: Zohar II 156a, Terumah — “'And I'—this is King David, the place called redemption. 'My prayer'—this is prayer, and here it is joined to redemption, for they are one. When he joins redemption to prayer, then it is a time of favor. 'A time of favor' is also one inclusive whole: time is one and favor is one, they are included in one another and become one. ... paragraphs.text: Zohar II 54a, Beshalach — “Rabbi Abba said: I considered all the praises with which they praised the Holy One, blessed be He, and all began with ‘Then’: ‘Then Solomon said’; ‘Then Joshua spoke’; ‘Then Israel sang.’ Why? paragraphs.text: Shemos Rabbah 22:3 — “One who reads the Shema must mention the splitting of the sea and the smiting of the firstborn in Emes VeYatziv. ... Why must one mention the splitting of the sea? Because when He split the sea for them, they believed in Him, as it is said: 'They believed in Hashem and in Moshe His servant.' Through their belief they merited to sing, and the Divine Presence rested upon them, for immediately afterward it is written: 'Then Moshe sang.' Therefore a person must join redemption to prayer, just as they joined song to faith and the splitting of the sea. Just as they purified their hearts and sang, so a person must purify his heart before praying.” The Midrash directly connects the sea's faith and song with the prayer order and the worshipper's purification of heart, the sequence that Rav Tzadok seeks to realize inwardly.

Now the term "laughter" is also found,
which our Sages, of blessed memory, applied
as it were, to Hashem Yisbarach,
In the last quarter of the day He sits and plays with the Leviathan,
And the Leviathan alludes to the yetzer hara
of desire, which is from the side of the serpent,
as they said in Midrash HaNe'elam
(זֹהַר חֵלֶק א קלז, א קלח, א)
will not be nullified even in the future,
for were it not for the evil inclination,
the joy of Torah learning would not be found;
for it has been whitened like one who bathes
And through the sin of Adam HaRishon,
in the mixing of good and evil,
there came to be in man's heart
a good inclination and an evil inclination.
"in the inclination of the thoughts of the heart of Your people";
and when it is directed to good,
it is called the good inclination.
And when King David, peace be upon him, saw
that they donated to the Mikdash
that this be preserved forever in the heart.
רַק הָאָדָם בְּעַצְמוֹ עוֹשֶׂה אוֹתוֹ רָע
Only man himself makes it evil,
to the desire of the body.
And when a person overcomes his inclination
and fights the battle of Hashem
as it were, with Hashem Yisbarach;
And our Sages, of blessed memory, also said
that one who did not watch
merits to see, in the World to Come,
of the Leviathan and the wild ox.
the sport of victory in battle
And we have already spoken about
the battle of the Leviathan and the wild ox
כִּי הַלִּוְיָתָן שׁוֹרֶשׁ יֵצֶר הָרַע דְּתַאֲוָה
that the Leviathan is the root of the yetzer hara of desire,
and the wild ox is the root
of the yetzer hara of anger and murder,

paragraphs.text: Zohar I 137a, 138a, Midrash HaNeelam — “At first, when it was sullied with sins in this world, it was called Lot. In the future, when it will no longer be sullied as at first, like one who bathes and immerses from impurity, they call it Lavan. In any event, the inclination is not abolished from the world. ... The inclination is needed by the world like rain is needed by the world: without it there would be no joy in learning a Torah teaching. But it will no longer be sullied as at first so as to sin through it, as it is written: 'They shall neither harm nor destroy on all My holy mountain.' Rabbi Shimon said: This is the heart, in which the inclination dwells.” The passage distinguishes desire's continuing life-giving energy from its sinful distortion. This distinction is essential to Rav Tzadok's account of the transformed inclination and the joy of Torah.

paragraphs.text: Midrash Tanchuma, Bereishis 7 — “The Holy One, blessed be He, Who is called righteous and upright, created the human being in His image only so that the person should be righteous and upright like Him. If you ask: Why did He create an evil inclination, of which it is written, 'The inclination of man's heart is evil from his youth'? You say that it is evil; who can make it good? The Holy One, blessed be He, said: You make it evil.” The Midrash locates responsibility for the inclination's evil in the person's development of it. Rav Tzadok accordingly distinguishes the original power of desire from its direction toward bodily indulgence.

paragraphs.text: Parallel: R. Shneur Zalman of Liadi, Tanya, Likkutei Amarim, chapter 27 — “There are two kinds of satisfaction before Him, blessed be He, above. One comes from the complete nullification of the Other Side and the transformation of bitterness into sweetness and darkness into light through the righteous. The second comes when the Other Side is subdued while it is still in its strength and might, raising itself like an eagle; from there Hashem brings it down through an awakening from below by the beinonim, those of intermediate spiritual standing. This is what Scripture says: ‘Make me delicacies as I love’—‘delicacies’ in the plural: two kinds of satisfaction. It is the Shechinah's address to her children, the community of Israel, as explained in the Tikkunim. In the analogy of bodily delicacies, there are two kinds of choice foods: one consists of pleasant, sweet foods, and the other of pungent or sour things, which are well seasoned and prepared until they become delicacies that restore the spirit.”

paragraphs.text: Vayikra Rabbah 13:3 — “Rabbi Yudan son of Rabbi Shimon said: Behemos and Leviathan will be the righteous people's spectacle in the future. Whoever has not watched the nations' spectacles in this world will merit to see it in the World to Come. How are they slaughtered? Behemos strikes Leviathan with its horns and tears it; Leviathan strikes Behemos with its fins and pierces it. The Sages asked: Is this valid slaughter? ... Rabbi Avin bar Kahana said: The Holy One, blessed be He, said, 'A new Torah shall go forth from Me'—a new disclosure of Torah shall go forth from Me.” The Midrash supplies the contest of the two creatures. Their identification with the roots of desire and anger, and the righteous person's purification of both, is Rav Tzadok's interpretation of that contest.

Rabbi Nasan permits it for two reasons: first, because one may cry out and save someone; second, because one may give testimony enabling a woman to marry.” The surrounding discussion treats public spectacles as a distraction from Torah and distinguishes the exceptional purpose of saving life or supplying testimony. Rav Tzadok cites this setting to explain the term kenigya for a contest or spectacle.

paragraphs.text: Bava Basra 74b — “Why not likewise castrate the male and cool the female? Fish are unrestrained. Why not do the reverse? One answer: a salted female is preferable. Another answer: since it is written, 'Leviathan, which You formed to play with,' it would not be fitting to play with a female.” The discussion concerns why the male and female Leviathan were prevented from reproducing together. Rav Tzadok takes the description of fish as sexually unrestrained into his symbolic account of Leviathan as the root of desire.

paragraphs.text: Berachos 61a — “Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak challenged: If so, does an animal, concerning which 'formed' is not written with two yuds, have no inclination? Yet we see that it injures, bites, and kicks! Rather, it is as Rabbi Shimon ben Pazi taught: Woe to me from my Creator, and woe to me from my inclination.” The objection points to aggression in animals. Rav Tzadok associates the beast's root here with anger and violence, distinguishing it from Leviathan's desire.

paragraphs.text: Shabbos 119b — “Rabbi Yosi bar Yehudah said: Two ministering angels accompany a person on Friday evening from the synagogue to his house, one good and one bad. When he enters his house and finds a lamp lit, the table prepared, and the bed arranged, the good angel says: May it be so on another Shabbos, and the bad angel answers Amen against its will. If not, the bad angel says: May it be so on another Shabbos, and the good angel answers Amen against its will.” The Gemara gives two accompanying angels. Their relation here to the wise heart on the right and foolish heart on the left is Rav Tzadok's interpretation of the opposing forces.

paragraphs.text: Avodah Zarah 3b — “In the third quarter He sits and nourishes the whole world, from the horns of the wild oxen to the eggs of lice. In the fourth quarter He sits and plays with Leviathan, as it is said: 'Leviathan, which You formed to play with.' Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak said: He plays with His creatures, but He laughs at His creatures only on that day.” The discussion then asks how this stands with the statement that, since the Temple's destruction, God has no laughter. It answers that in the fourth quarter He sits and teaches Torah to schoolchildren, applying 'Whom shall He teach knowledge? ... Those weaned from milk.' This change of activity is the textual basis for Rav Tzadok's contrast between mastery of the inclination and the children's sinless Torah.

paragraphs.text: Zohar III 160a, Shelach — “Furthermore, ‘Amalek dwells in the land of the Negev.’ If a person says that despite all this he will attain it: ‘Amalek dwells in the land of the Negev’—this is the evil inclination, the accuser, who accuses a person and is constantly found in the body. ‘The Hittite and the Amorite’—how many accusers are found there, so that a person cannot enter that world at all. Who will merit it, and who will enter it? With these words ‘they disheartened the children of Israel,’ for they brought out an evil report about it.” The Zohar first portrays the discouraging accusation, then answers it with sincere will and guarding the covenant. This exact context supports Rav Tzadok's identification of Amalek as the accusing root of the inclination.
